source: Battambang Provincial Department of Agriculture and the Cambodia Northwest Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee (financial support from the SEILA Programme), Khmer translation of Photpeechon Whayooathdee, "ដំណាំខ្នុរ (Jackfruit)", "Translation Copy No. 4", January 1997 (500 copies printed). This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. Cover illustration source: Forestry/Fuelwood Research and Development Project, 1992, "Growing Multipurpose Trees on Small Farms", Winrock International, Bangkok. Other artwork by Sarath, Som, Center for Social Development, Phnom Penh, Dec. 1996.
text:
This chapter focuses specifically on growing jackfruit in home/dooryard gardens rather than commercial orchard blocks, reflecting that this is how most Cambodian and regional households actually keep jackfruit trees. It discusses selecting a suitable spot near the house that gives the tree room to reach full size (the text repeats the concern from earlier chapters that jackfruit trees grow very large, so planting too close to buildings, fences, or power lines is discouraged), while also taking advantage of household organic waste and wastewater as a convenient nutrient and water source for the tree.

The chapter gives more specific fertilizer program guidance appropriate to a small number of dooryard trees, again referencing standard compound fertilizer ratios (the source lists several example formulations such as 15-15-15, 16-16-16, 20-20-20, and 12-3-6, applied at different growth/fruiting stages) alongside household compost and manure, with quantities and timing adjusted to the size and age of the tree and the intensity of fruiting expected that year.

Two further practical topics are covered in detail in this chapter under named sub-headings in the source:
- Termite control ("ធាតុគ្រែសែន" section): the text describes termite damage risk to jackfruit trunks and roots, particularly in trees weakened by other stress, and gives control approaches including keeping the base of the tree clear of dead wood/mulch that attracts termites and applying appropriate soil/trunk treatments when termite activity is found.
- Weed control ("ធាតុសំណប់ដី" section): the text discusses controlling weeds around the base of young and mature trees to reduce competition for water and nutrients and to reduce habitat for pests, describing manual weeding and mulching around the tree base as the main recommended methods for home gardens, as opposed to broad herbicide use.

The chapter also gives brief general guidance on maintaining tree vigor in a home-garden setting: regular observation for pest or disease problems, maintaining soil moisture, and periodic light pruning to keep the tree a manageable and productive shape near the home.
